# Commit messages

The diff says *what changed*. The commit message exists to say *why*. This file is the deep dive for principle 3 of [[git-workflow]] — the format, the conventions, and the anti-patterns.

## Table of contents

- [Conventional commits at a glance](#conventional-commits-at-a-glance)
- [Subject line — the contract with future readers](#subject-line)
- [Body — the why, the shape, the trade-off](#body)
- [Footers — issues, breaking changes, co-authors](#footers)

## Conventional commits at a glance

The format:

```
<type>(<scope>): <subject>

<body>

<footers>
```

**What the spec actually requires.** Conventional Commits v1.0.0 mandates only **`feat`** and **`fix`**. Every other type — including the Angular set (`build|chore|ci|docs|perf|refactor|style|test`) and project-specific ones like `spike` — is *project-local*. Pick a type list, write it down, and hold the line; do not assume readers know your particular set. Tools that parse Conventional Commits care only about `feat`, `fix`, and the `!`/`BREAKING CHANGE:` marker for major versions.

Types this project uses (mirroring `/dev` run types so the log and the workflow speak the same language):

| Type | When | Spec status |
|---|---|---|
| `feat` | New user-visible capability | **Mandatory** in CC v1.0.0 |
| `fix` | Bug fix — pairs with a regression test | **Mandatory** in CC v1.0.0 |
| `refactor` | Internal restructure, no behavior change | Angular convention |
| `perf` | Performance change, no behavior change | Angular convention |
| `chore` | Tooling, deps, infra, nothing user-facing | Angular convention |
| `docs` | Documentation only | Angular convention |
| `test` | Tests only (added or fixed; no production code change) | Angular convention |
| `build` | Build system, package manifests, CI manifest | Angular convention |
| `ci` | CI configuration only | Angular convention |
| `spike` | Exploratory work, may or may not ship | **Project-local** (matches `/dev` run types) |
| `revert` | Reverts a prior commit (auto-generated by `git revert`) | Angular convention |

Scope is optional but extremely useful — it's usually the module, package, or feature area (`auth`, `audit`, `orders`, `cli`, `installer`). Keep scopes consistent across the repo; the same scope every time is worth more than a slightly better scope each time.

## Subject line

The subject line is the part everyone reads. It must stand alone in `git log --oneline`, in PR titles, in changelog tools, in `git blame` summaries.

**Rules:**
- ≤72 characters total (including type + scope + colon).
- Imperative mood — "Add audit log", not "Added" / "Adding" / "Adds." Read it as "If applied, this commit will ___".
- No trailing period.
- Lowercase after the colon (this is a convention, not a law — match what the repo already does).
- Specific. "fix(auth): handle empty session" beats "fix(auth): bug fix."

**Good subjects:**
```
feat(audit): record user_id on every audit row
fix(auth): persist session before redirect to fix login loop
refactor(orders): pull formatter through (no behavior change)
perf(query): index orders.user_id for the dashboard lookup
chore(deps): bump axios 1.6.0 → 1.7.2
docs: add /dev troubleshooting section to WORKFLOW.md
```

**Bad subjects:**
```
update                     ← what?
fix                         ← which bug?
WIP                         ← don't ship WIP commits to main
Fixed the thing             ← past tense; "the thing" is not a thing
Added a feature             ← past tense; which feature?
Some refactoring + a bug fix ← two commits, not one
```

## Body

The body explains *why* the change exists and any non-obvious shape decisions.

**When to write a body:** any commit where a future reader would reasonably ask "why?" or "why this way?" — which is almost every non-trivial commit. Skip the body only when the subject is genuinely complete on its own (`docs: fix typo in README`).

**Rules:**
- Separate from the subject by one blank line.
- Wrap at ~72 chars per line for readability in terminals and `git log`.
- Explain *why* and *what the shape is*, not *what the diff is*. The diff is right there.
- Mention alternatives you considered and rejected, when interesting. "Chose X over Y because Y would have broken the staging cache" is gold for the next engineer.
- Reference the failing test, the runbook, the design doc, the incident — by ID, not paraphrase.

**Good body:**
```
fix(auth): persist session before redirect to fix login loop

When the OAuth callback set the session cookie and immediately
redirected, Chrome (but not Firefox) dropped the cookie on the
cross-origin redirect. Flush the session write before redirecting
so the Set-Cookie header has committed by the time the 302 fires.

Considered moving the redirect into a meta-refresh on a landing page;
rejected because it adds a visible flash on every login.

Regression test: auth.spec.ts:redirect-loop.
Closes #482.
```

## Footers

Footers are machine-readable trailers at the bottom of the message. They're parsed by changelog tools, issue trackers, and CI.

Common footers:

```
Closes #482
Fixes #482
Refs #482
Co-authored-by: Name <email@example.com>
Reviewed-by: Name <email@example.com>
BREAKING CHANGE: <description>
```

Use the verb that matches the relationship: `Closes` / `Fixes` to autoclose an issue on merge, `Refs` to link without closing.

## Breaking changes

Two equivalent forms:

```
feat(api)!: replace /v1/orders payload with the v2 shape

BREAKING CHANGE: clients on /v1 must migrate. See MIGRATION.md.
```

or just the `!` after the type if the body already explains it:

```
feat(api)!: replace /v1/orders payload with the v2 shape
```

Changelog tools key off the `!` *and* the `BREAKING CHANGE:` footer; the redundancy is fine. **Never** ship a silent breaking change — if it breaks a consumer, the consumer's owner should be able to grep the log for `BREAKING` and find it.

## Anti-patterns

| Anti-pattern | Why it's bad | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| "WIP" / "fix" / "stuff" | Useless to anyone who didn't write it | Fold into the real commit via `git commit --amend` or `git rebase -i` before pushing |
| "Address PR feedback" | The PR is a transient artifact; the message survives forever | Describe what you actually changed: "fix(auth): use --force-with-lease, not --force, per review" |
| Past tense ("Added", "Fixed") | Style guide says imperative; tooling expects it | "Add" / "Fix" |
| Mixing types ("feat + fix + chore in one commit") | Bisect and revert become impossible | Split into separate commits via `git add -p` |
| `git commit -m "fix"` (no body) on a substantive change | Loses the why permanently | Write the body. Future you will thank current you. |
| Pasted error message as the entire body | The diff probably already shows what; this hides the why | Translate: "X failed because Y, fixed by Z" |
| 500-character subject because "it didn't fit" | Truncated everywhere — log, PR title, blame view | The commit is two commits. Split. |

## Project-specific conventions

This project's `/dev` workflow types directly map to commit types — when a `/dev` run produces a commit, the type comes from the spec's `Type:` slot. That's the source of truth for whether a change is a `feat`, `fix`, `refactor`, etc.

The engineer agent's ship step references the run ID in the body, e.g.:

```
feat(audit): record user_id on every audit row

Adds nullable user_id column populated from the request session.
Falls back to "system" for callback-driven writes (cron, webhooks).

Run: 0007-feat-audit-actor
Change: openspec/changes/add-audit-actor/
```

That gives `git log` a one-way link back into the workflow folder where the spec, plan, review, and retro live forever.
